messages.content:
You are verifying one structured PFAS study evidence record against the
complete source evidence cited by that record.

You receive:
1. the review task and task-specific extraction objective;
2. the held-out anchor identifiers;
3. one extracted evidence record; and
4. the complete source chunks or inspected source-page text referenced by the
   record.

Judge only source support and transcription. Do not reward usefulness,
verbosity, or agreement with general background knowledge.

Assess every substantive populated source-dependent field against only its
attached field-level locators. Do not create separate assessments for locator
arrays, record IDs, or formatting metadata:
- supported: the cited evidence directly supports the field and its material
  qualifiers;
- partially_supported: the core statement is supported but a material
  qualifier, condition, denominator, or scope is missing;
- unsupported: the cited evidence does not establish the field;
- contradicted: the cited evidence directly conflicts with the field.

For quantitative_findings, value must contain an actual number, censored or
approximate number, range, or explicit ND/not-detected result. A unit-shaped
string such as "nmol/L" in value with an empty unit is a unit error even when
the source mentions that concentration scale. Do not silently reinterpret one
schema field as another. Confirm that value matches value_form; explanatory
text and uncertainty belong in qualifiers.

Classify endpoint_type from the measured basis, not the source's terminology.
Parent-compound loss alone is not destruction; phase transfer is not
degradation; inorganic fluoride release or fluorine-balance closure establishes
defluorination but not mineralization. Mineralization requires direct
carbon-fate evidence such as measured CO2/inorganic carbon or a carbon balance.
If an author calls defluorination mineralization without that evidence, retain
the author phrase only as reported_term and mark endpoint_type=mineralization
unsupported with error_type=endpoint_classification.

Comparability is an analyst-derived judgment. Do not require the source to
state the comparability conclusion verbatim. Instead, judge whether its status
and reason follow conservatively from supported cited fields for matrix, PFAS
scope, scale, conditions, endpoint, unit, and denominator.

An author_reported limitation requires direct source support. A
design_inferred limitation is supported when it follows necessarily from
cited design facts; absence from the supplied packet is not a study
limitation.

Classify errors as numeric_transcription, unit, qualifier,
endpoint_classification, source_attribution, other, or none. A record is usable
only if its source identity, matrix, treatment, endpoints, and quantitative
findings are not unsupported or contradicted in a way that would mislead
  synthesis. A usable record can still contain non-core fields that synthesis
must exclude according to their field assessments.

For metric consistency, always emit separate assessments with these exact
field-path forms when the corresponding item exists:
- `quantitative_findings[i].value`;
- `quantitative_findings[i].unit`;
- `operating_conditions[i].value`;
- `operating_conditions[i].unit`;
- `endpoints[i].endpoint_type`; and
- `comparability.status`.

Other substantive fields may be assessed individually or as a whole object,
but do not omit these required assessment types and do not emit a required
field path more than once.

Report anchor_exclusion_violation=true if the source resolves to any held-out
anchor DOI, URL, exact title, or corpus source.

Return one JSON object that follows the supplied verification schema exactly.

field_assessments.reason: The record DOI/URL exactly matches the DOI given in the source metadata (10.1016/j.jhazmat.2026.141033; https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhazmat.2026.141033).

The abstract describes removal of 17 different PFAS from "contaminated water" (S05-E05). The dataset was compiled from studies found with keywords including "wastewater" and "removal" (S05-E06), and PFAS removal from wastewater is also mentioned elsewhere (S05-E04). Describing the matrix as contaminated water / wastewater from multiple NF/RO PFAS studies is consistent with these locators.

The abstract states that the study analyzes the performance of "24 types of RO and NF membranes" for removing PFAS (S05-E05). The conclusion specifies the dataset includes "6 commercial NF membranes, 9 commercial RO membranes, and 9 modified membranes" (S05-E06). The treatment description of membrane-based treatment using 24 NF/RO membranes with those counts is directly supported.

The conclusion reports that 18 relevant papers provided 480 experimental data points and that the dataset encompassed 17 different PFAS species and multiple NF/RO membranes (S05-E06). Combined with the abstract’s description of a machine-learning model of PFAS removal (S05-E03, S05-E05), describing this as a data-driven modeling study using 480 data points for 17 PFAS from 18 prior lab studies is accurate.

The work develops and optimizes a kernel extreme learning machine (KELM) model using SSA and AdaBoost to predict PFAS removal by NF/RO membranes (S05-E03, S05-E05, S05-E07). This clearly falls under a modeling study rather than a new bench-scale experiment, so classifying it as "modeling_or_life_cycle_study" is supported.

The abstract and title focus on "PFAS removal" from contaminated water via membrane-based treatment (S05-E03, S05-E05), and discuss membrane rejection efficiency and its dependence on various factors (S05-E06, S05-E08). Modeling of rejection/removal efficiency is therefore correctly classified under the endpoint_type "removal".

The study evaluates machine-learning model performance using metrics such as R2 and RMSE for predicting PFAS removal efficiency (S05-E03, S05-E05, S05-E07). These are model performance endpoints, not treatment performance metrics per se, so classifying this as endpoint_type "other" is appropriate and supported.

The source explicitly notes that the main issue of data in membrane science involves "limited dataset size, high variance, diverse data sources, and complex systems" and that ML algorithms require further optimization (S05-E04). This matches the author-reported limitation description.

The conclusion states that the dataset was compiled from 18 papers, yielding 480 experimental data points and that a table summarized source paper, membrane type, testing configuration, feed matrix, and PFAS species (S05-E06). From this design, it is reasonable to infer heterogeneity in feed matrices, configurations, and membrane types, and thus that modeled effects cannot be attributed to standardized matrix comparisons. This is a valid design-inferred limitation.

The results emphasize that influent conditions such as PFAS concentration, pH, inorganic ions, and operating pressure directly influence membrane performance and PFAS removal (S05-E02, S05-E08). However, the excerpt does not provide specific constituent concentrations nor controlled clean- vs real-water comparisons. Inferring that this limits direct inference on water-matrix effects is a reasonable design-based interpretation of the cited text.

The abstract notes analysis of "24 types of RO and NF membranes" (S05-E05), and the conclusion specifies the dataset included "6 commercial NF membranes, 9 commercial RO membranes, and 9 modified membranes" (S05-E06). The value string accurately reproduces these numbers.
The field describes a count and types of membranes, not a numeric quantity needing a measurement unit. Leaving unit as null is appropriate and consistent with the source (S05-E05, S05-E06).

The value is intentionally left empty, with qualifiers explaining that PFAS concentration is treated as an influent condition without a numeric range in the excerpt. The results text confirms that "the influent conditions, including the concentration of PFAS" affect removal (S05-E08). Thus, representing this as a named condition without a numeric value is consistent with the available text.
No quantitative concentration values are provided in the cited text (S05-E08), so leaving the unit as null is appropriate.

The pH condition is mentioned qualitatively, with no numeric values given. The results explain that variations in pH alter PFAS charge state and influence removal (S05-E02, S05-E08). Using an empty value and capturing pH as a qualitative operating condition is consistent with the source.
Numerical pH values are not reported in the provided excerpt (S05-E02, S05-E08), so a null unit is appropriate.

Inorganic ions in the influent (e.g., calcium) are discussed as affecting PFAS removal via complexation (S05-E02) and are listed among influent conditions (S05-E08), but no concentrations are provided. Representing this as a qualitative condition with an empty value is consistent with the text.
Since no numeric concentrations of inorganic ions are reported (S05-E02, S05-E08), the null unit is appropriate.

Operating pressure is identified as an operating condition that must be optimized (S05-E02) and is included among influent conditions (S05-E08), but no numeric pressures are given. Leaving the value empty while naming the condition matches the qualitative information provided.
No pressure values or units are reported in the cited text (S05-E02, S05-E08), so it is correct to have a null unit.

The abstract notes that "twelve characteristic variables were selected as model inputs" based on removal mechanisms and operating conditions (S05-E05). The methods section discusses key feature variables without listing all of them (S05-E07). Capturing this as other influent/operating conditions with an unspecified list and empty value is aligned with the excerpt.
This field aggregates several qualitative model input variables rather than a single measured quantity, and no units are given in the source (S05-E05, S05-E07). A null unit is therefore appropriate.

The conclusion reports that the compiled dataset encompassed 17 PFAS species and that targets were grouped into three PFAS classes, one being perfluoroalkyl sulfonic acids (PFSAs) (S05-E06). Stating that 17 PFAS species include PFSAs is consistent with this description.
Perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids (PFCAs) are listed as one of the three PFAS classes into which target PFAS were grouped (S05-E06). The extracted value matches the source terminology.
Perfluoroether carboxylic acids (PFECAs) are the third PFAS class named in the conclusion (S05-E06). The extracted scope value directly reflects this.

The abstract reports that the baseline KELM model delivered accuracy with "R 2 = 0.56" (S05-E05), and the methods section repeats that the baseline KELM achieved R2 of 0.56 on the test set (S05-E07). The recorded value 0.56 matches exactly and is correctly typed as exact_numeric.
R2 is a dimensionless statistical metric; no unit is given in the source (S05-E05, S05-E07). Using a null unit is correct.

The abstract states that the baseline KELM model had "RMSE = 10.31" (S05-E05), and the methods section confirms RMSE = 10.31 on the test set (S05-E07). The extracted numeric value 10.31 is accurate and typed as exact_numeric.

RMSE is reported numerically without an explicit unit; it implicitly follows the scale of the response variable (rejection percent), but the paper does not specify a unit for RMSE (S05-E05, S05-E07). Leaving unit null is appropriate.

The methods section reports that SSA optimization improved R2 to 0.71 for the test set (S05-E07). The extracted value 0.71 for SSA-optimized KELM R2 matches this number exactly and is correctly marked as exact_numeric.
As with other R2 metrics, this is dimensionless and no unit is provided in the source (S05-E07). Null unit is correct.

The abstract gives the optimized SSA-AdaBoost KELM predictive performance as "R 2 = 0.85" (S05-E05), and the methods section confirms R2 = 0.85 on the test set after SSA plus AdaBoost (S05-E07). The recorded value 0.85 is an exact transcription.
This is again an R2 value, which is dimensionless; no unit is reported in the source (S05-E05, S05-E07). Null unit is appropriate.

The abstract and methods both state that the SSA-AdaBoost optimized model achieved "RMSE = 5.04" on the test data (S05-E05, S05-E07). The extracted value 5.04 matches exactly and is correctly labeled exact_numeric.
RMSE is reported as a pure number without an explicit unit (S05-E05, S05-E07). Leaving the unit null is consistent with the source.

The dataset is compiled from 18 different papers, with 480 data points, multiple membrane types, testing configurations, and feed matrices summarized in Table S1 (S05-E06). The paper analyzes PFAS removal as a function of many variables (S05-E02, S05-E08) and develops ML models (S05-E03, S05-E05) but does not describe controlled, matched clean-water vs. matrix-modified experiments. From this, judging the record as "not_comparable" to controlled matrix-effect studies is a reasonable, supported inference.

result.record_usable_rationale: Core elements—source identity, PFAS treatment via NF/RO membranes, matrix description, modeling-based study scale, endpoint classification, and all quantitative model performance metrics—are directly supported by the cited text with no transcription or unit errors. Any interpretive limitations are clearly labeled as design-inferred and do not compromise the basic factual content. The record is therefore suitable for synthesis, while recognizing it represents a secondary modeling analysis rather than primary controlled matrix-effect experiments.
